body:
The three inputs converge on a point worth holding: the material does not establish which mechanism is driving the disputes. The original account treats the memory gap as central; the objection reverses that ordering and puts avoidance at the load-bearing position; the rival holds three readings side by side and proposes a probe before any intervention. I take the convergence on underdetermination as the strongest shared ground.

What I will use: the rival's probe — asking each flatmate separately what they thought a past agreement meant — because it is low-cost, does not presume a solution, and could discriminate between the memory-gap, scope-ambiguity, and standing-negotiation readings. I will also use the objection's distinction between memorial and normative disagreement, because it clarifies what a written record can and cannot settle. From the original account, I retain the proposal to approach the avoiding friend, but I revise its framing in light of the objection and rival: the conversation should not treat avoidance as a problem to correct but as information to gather about what the group conversations cost them.

What I will leave open: whether a written record is the right next step after the probe. The objection is correct that a record may relocate rather than resolve disagreement if the underlying issue is normative (what counts as done, how often, whether it is a role). I will also leave open whether the avoidance predates the schedule changes or follows them; the material does not say, and treating my inference as fact would repeat the error the objection names.

What I will reject: the slide from 'no shared record' to 'make a shared record' as if the diagnosis were established. All three inputs caution against this in different ways, and the caution is warranted. I also reject treating the one-to-one conversation with the avoiding friend as clearly correct without attention to framing; if the avoidance is a response to being unheard in the group, a private conversation can reproduce that dynamic at smaller scale.

The grounds for these decisions are internal to the material provided: the problem statement names three elements (disagreements about meaning, changing schedules, avoidance) but does not rank them or establish causation. Any intervention that assumes a ranking risks solving the wrong problem. The probe does not assume a ranking; it gathers data that could support one reading over another. That is why it comes first.
commitments:
Taking this up involves several distinct commitments, each revisable independently.

First, a methodological commitment: I am treating the probe (asking each flatmate what they thought a past agreement meant) as a data-gathering step rather than as a solution. Its value is in discriminating between competing readings, not in resolving the dispute directly. If the probe returns no clustering around scope, recurrence, or timing, that weakens the memory-gap and scope-ambiguity readings and gives more weight to the standing-negotiation reading. I commit to treating that outcome as informative rather than as failure.

Second, a diagnostic commitment: I am holding the three readings (memory gap, scope ambiguity at moment of agreement, arguments as standing-negotiation) as live possibilities rather than settling on one. This is a claim about what the material supports, not about what is happening in the flat. If subsequent information establishes one reading decisively, this commitment should be revised.

Third, an intervention commitment: I am proposing the written record as a conditional next step, dependent on what the probe reveals. If the probe shows disputes cluster around 'what was agreed,' a record may help. If they cluster around 'what counts as done' or 'how often,' a record without scope definition may relocate the disagreement. I commit to not treating the record as a standalone remedy.

Fourth, a framing commitment for the avoiding-friend conversation: I am proposing the question be framed as 'what do the group conversations cost you?' rather than 'why do you avoid them?' This inherits the uncertainty of the readings above — if avoidance is not about the group dynamic, this framing may miss the mark. I commit to treating a negative response as data about the framing, not as resistance to be overcome.

Unresolved: I do not know whether the household would tolerate a probe, whether the avoiding friend will speak one-to-one, or whether the disputes are symmetric. I am not claiming the probe is risk-free; asking about past disagreements may itself be read as interrogation. I am proposing it because its cost is lower than implementing a system based on an untested diagnosis, not because it is certain to help.

What I am not committing to: I am not endorsing the standing-negotiation reading as true, not claiming a mediator is necessary, not asserting that the written record is wrong in principle, and not ranking the three readings by likelihood. Those would exceed what the material supports.
